lesson.title: Only the Useful Bytes: Why Goodput Is the Number That Matters
lesson.summary: Goodput is the rate at which actual, useful application data arrives, excluding protocol headers and retransmitted or discarded packets, making it consistently the lowest and most honest of the three related measures: bandwidth, throughput, and goodput.
lesson.body:
Throughput counts every bit that successfully crosses a link within some time window, including protocol headers, retransmitted copies of packets that were lost the first time, and any other overhead the transport and network layers add along the way. Goodput narrows that further to only the bits that represent genuinely new, useful application data, the bytes actually delivered to and usable by whatever application is receiving the transfer. The relationship among the three measures forms a strict hierarchy: goodput is less than or equal to throughput, which is in turn less than or equal to bandwidth, since each step subtracts something that the previous measure still counted.

The gap between throughput and goodput becomes especially visible on unreliable links. Consider a wireless connection experiencing significant interference, forcing frequent retransmissions of lost frames. A throughput measurement at the radio layer might report a healthy 50 Mbps of bits successfully transmitted over the air, but if half of those bits are retransmissions of frames that had to be sent two or three times before arriving correctly, the goodput, the rate of actually new data reaching the application, might be closer to 25 Mbps. The throughput number is not wrong, it accurately counts everything that crossed the link, but it overstates how fast useful work is actually getting done.

A file transfer example makes the layered relationship concrete. Suppose a 100 MB file is downloaded over a connection with a measured throughput of 100 Mbps. Ethernet, IP, and TCP headers on every packet consume a small percentage of that raw rate without carrying any file content, so goodput is already slightly below the throughput just from routine overhead. If the path also experiences some packet loss, requiring TCP to retransmit a portion of the segments, those retransmitted bytes count toward throughput, since they did successfully cross the link, but they do not represent new file content, since the data they carry duplicates something already sent. The result might be an effective goodput of, say, 80 Mbps for that particular transfer, meaningfully below both the link's 100 Mbps bandwidth and its measured throughput.

Goodput is ultimately the number that matters most to a user waiting for a download to finish or a video to buffer, because it is the only one of the three that directly reflects useful progress rather than raw activity on the wire. Engineers optimizing real systems, choosing more efficient headers, tuning retransmission behavior, reducing unnecessary protocol chatter, are, whether they use the word or not, almost always trying to push goodput closer to the throughput and bandwidth that set its ceiling.

Packet size affects this ratio too, since header overhead is fixed per packet regardless of how much payload that packet carries. A stream of many small packets, common in interactive traffic like voice calls, pays the fixed header cost far more often relative to the useful bytes delivered than a stream of large packets carrying a big file does, so goodput as a fraction of throughput tends to run lower for small-packet traffic than for bulk transfers, all else being equal.
